common_name: Sandstorm Prairieblues Baptisia (Bicolor Sandy-Yellow and Violet False Indigo Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into deep, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a permanent spot since the deep taproot resents later disturbance.

directions: Sandstorm is a second-generation Baptisia australis x bracteata hybrid bred at the Chicago Botanic Garden as part of the Prairieblues program, chosen for its unusually profuse bicolor flowers that open sandy-yellow marked with violet and fade softly as they age. The long flower spikes, often reaching close to two feet, stand well above a broad, dense mound of blue-green foliage that keeps expanding through the season into a rounded clump. It blooms for roughly three weeks in mid-spring and draws abundant bumblebee and native bee activity. Once settled on its permanent site, it needs no staking, feeding, or division, tolerating heat and drought with ease.

common_name: Midnight Prairieblues Baptisia (Two-Flush Deep Violet-Blue False Indigo Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into deep, well-drained soil in full sun, selecting a permanent location since mature plants dislike being moved or divided.

directions: Another Chicago Botanic Garden Prairieblues introduction, Midnight is notable for producing two separate bloom flushes: a long primary spike of deep blue-violet flowers in late spring followed by shorter secondary spikes that extend color into early summer. Its upright, vase-shaped clump of fine-textured green foliage holds its form well into autumn before coloring with the first hard frost. The saturated violet-blue flower color is especially rich compared with many blue-flowered Baptisia selections, making it a strong anchor plant for pollinator borders. Established clumps are extremely drought-tolerant and require essentially no routine maintenance.

common_name: Last Dance Baptisia (Late-Blooming White-to-Cream False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall into average to poor, well-drained garden soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site to avoid disturbing the taproot later.

directions: Selected from the Chicago Botanic Garden's accredited Baptisia collection, Last Dance stands out for flowering noticeably later than other cultivars in the genus, with buds opening white and gradually warming to pale creamy yellow over an extended late spring to early summer display. Its many upright, bare-based stems give the clump a tidy, almost columnar look in bud that broadens into a rounded mound equal in width and height once fully leafed out. The light green summer foliage turns a dramatic near-black after the first fall frost, adding a second season of visual interest. It tolerates poor and average soils alike and, once established, needs no division, staking, or regular watering.

planting.note: Use only nursery-propagated seed or stock and sow or transplant in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, mimicking its native scrub and sandhill habitat.

directions: Hairy Florida wild indigo is a sprawling, multi-branched species confined to sandhills and dry pine woodland of the Florida panhandle and nearby Alabama, listed as a threatened species in Florida. Unlike the blue, purple, yellow, or white flowers typical of most Baptisia, it produces unusual brick-red to peachy orange blooms on long, spreading branches, making it visually distinct within the genus and valuable as an unusual nectar source for native bees. It thrives only in lean, excessively well-drained sandy soil in full sun and does poorly in rich or moisture-retentive garden beds, so it suits dedicated sandhill or xeric native plantings rather than typical perennial borders. As with other narrow-range Baptisia species, gardeners should source only nursery-propagated material rather than wild-collected plants.
